prohibited_recommendations: Do NOT delay empiric antimicrobial therapy while awaiting imaging or LP results when bacterial meningitis is clinically suspected.
Do not perform lumbar puncture before cranial imaging in this patient: new-onset seizures in an adult is an imaging-first criterion under WHO 2025 section A.4.
Do NOT rely on a negative Gram stain or a 'normal CT' to rule out bacterial meningitis when the clinical syndrome is present.
Do not exclude bacterial meningitis on a near-normal CSF white cell count when the multiplex PCR or the blood cultures identify a bacterial pathogen.
Do NOT treat with oral antibiotics alone; CNS penetration is inadequate for meningitis.
Do not use enzyme-inducing antiseizure medicines (carbamazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbital) with efavirenz: they lower antiretroviral levels.
required_recommendations: Give ceftriaxone 2 g IV every 12 hours (or cefotaxime 2 g IV every 6 hours) within 60 minutes of clinical suspicion, after blood cultures and without waiting for imaging or lumbar puncture (WHO 2025, strong recommendation). Add vancomycin only where pneumococcal resistance to penicillin or third-generation cephalosporins is highly prevalent locally (WHO 2025, conditional recommendation).
Add ampicillin 2 g IV every 4 hours for Listeria monocytogenes cover because of HIV infection, an immunocompromised state (WHO 2025, strong recommendation).

Do not give adjunctive dexamethasone by default: WHO 2025 extends its corticosteroid recommendation to people living with HIV only when they are on antiretroviral therapy with an undetectable viral load (below 50 copies/mL); his viral load is 4850 copies/mL after 2 months of therapy, and adjunctive corticosteroids have not proven beneficial in advanced HIV disease (WHO 2025).
Draw two sets of peripheral blood cultures before the first antibiotic dose.

Take blood cultures and give the first dose of empirical antibiotics before cranial imaging; obtain a CT head before lumbar puncture because of new-onset seizures in an adult (WHO 2025 section A.4); neither imaging nor lumbar puncture may delay treatment.

Send full CSF panel (cell count, differential, glucose, protein, Gram stain, culture, meningitis multiplex PCR, lactate) at the LP, with cryptococcal antigen, AFB smear, Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra and VDRL in this HIV-infected patient.

Narrow therapy once the organism and susceptibilities are known: Streptococcus pneumoniae susceptible to penicillin (MIC 0.06 mg/L) and ceftriaxone; stop ampicillin and continue ceftriaxone, or switch to benzylpenicillin, for 14 days.
Place patient on droplet precautions until meningococcal disease is excluded.
Treat the new seizures with levetiracetam, which does not interact with efavirenz.

Continue antiretroviral therapy, co-trimoxazole prophylaxis and fluconazole secondary prophylaxis; review adherence, since he misses fluconazole doses and the viral load is still detectable (4850 copies/mL) after 2 months of treatment.
Reassess the right frontal lesion with repeat contrast MRI after treatment of the meningitis; if it persists or enlarges, send CSF JC virus PCR and toxoplasma serology.
Arrange formal audiological assessment before discharge, or within 4 weeks of discharge if it cannot be done before (WHO 2025, strong recommendation).

key_clinical_evidence: Acute bacterial meningitis presents with fever, headache, meningismus, and altered mental status; the full triad is present in only ~40%, so partial syndromes warrant aggressive workup.
Antibiotics are given within 60 minutes of suspicion; neither imaging nor lumbar puncture may delay them (WHO 2025).

Take blood cultures and give the first dose of empirical antibiotics before cranial imaging; obtain a CT head before lumbar puncture because of new-onset seizures in an adult (WHO 2025 section A.4); neither imaging nor lumbar puncture may delay treatment.

Do not give adjunctive dexamethasone by default: WHO 2025 extends its corticosteroid recommendation to people living with HIV only when they are on antiretroviral therapy with an undetectable viral load (below 50 copies/mL); his viral load is 4850 copies/mL after 2 months of therapy, and adjunctive corticosteroids have not proven beneficial in advanced HIV disease (WHO 2025).

A negative Gram stain does not exclude bacterial meningitis: sensitivity is about 85% with wide confidence limits (WHO 2025), lower after antibiotics; culture and multiplex PCR establish the organism.

A CSF:blood glucose ratio of 0.4 or less is abnormally low (WHO 2025 A.2.2) and is more informative than the absolute value, above all in hyperglycemia; a normal ratio, as here (0.55), does not exclude bacterial meningitis.

Empirical therapy is ceftriaxone or cefotaxime within 60 minutes, with ampicillin when a Listeria risk factor (age over 60, pregnancy, immunocompromise) is present; vancomycin only where pneumococcal resistance is locally prevalent (WHO 2025).

A near-normal CSF white cell count does not exclude bacterial meningitis: here 3 cells/uL with protein 204.7 mg/dL in a man taking daily co-trimoxazole, which has antipneumococcal activity and partially treats the infection; the multiplex PCR and the blood cultures identify Streptococcus pneumoniae.

In a person with HIV, a new parenchymal lesion found on imaging for meningitis is characterized by contrast MRI and followed up after treatment; without midline shift or basal cistern effacement it does not contraindicate lumbar puncture.

sequence_constraints.reason: Under WHO 2025 section A.4 cranial imaging is not performed routinely; where readily accessible it precedes lumbar puncture when any of these is present at presentation: Glasgow Coma Score below 10, focal neurological signs, cranial nerve deficits, papilledema, new-onset seizures in adults, or a severe immunocompromised state. Here: new-onset seizures in an adult (two witnessed episodes of staring with arm stiffening in the past week); a CD4 count of 312 is not a severe immunocompromised state. NICE NG240 does not cover this patient (HIV infection is an immunodeficiency outside its scope). Blood cultures and the first antibiotic dose with dexamethasone come before imaging, which must not delay them.

patient.history_present_illness:
Mr. Okonkwo is a 42-year-old right-handed man with known HIV infection diagnosed three years ago who presents to the emergency department with a one-day history of worsening headache, confusion and restlessness. He was hospitalized two months prior at an outside facility for a similar presentation of headache and altered mental status, where he was treated empirically with intravenous ceftriaxone for presumed bacterial meningitis and high-dose fluconazole for possible cryptococcal meningitis. At that time, he was also initiated on antiretroviral therapy with tenofovir, lamivudine, and efavirenz, along with co-trimoxazole prophylaxis. His CD4 count at the prior admission was 359 cells per cubic millimeter. He reports partial improvement after the initial hospitalization and was discharged with instructions to continue his antiretroviral regimen and fluconazole prophylaxis.

Over the past two weeks, his wife has noticed progressive changes in his behavior, including increased irritability, occasional episodes of inappropriate laughter, and difficulty with everyday tasks that he previously performed without difficulty. He has been sleeping poorly and appears restless at night. Three days ago, he developed a dull, diffuse headache that has gradually worsened. Yesterday, he became noticeably confused, unable to recall recent conversations, and more agitated than usual. His wife brought him to the emergency department today when he appeared increasingly disoriented.

The patient reports that he has had a persistent ulcer on the inside of his right cheek near the molar area for approximately three weeks. He has not sought dental care for this lesion and has been managing it with saltwater rinses. He also notes intermittent mild right jaw swelling that he attributes to bruxism during sleep. He denies any recent fever, though his wife recalls that he felt warm to the touch during his prior hospitalization. He denies cough, shortness of breath at rest, abdominal pain, urinary symptoms, rash, or joint pains. He has taken his antiretroviral medications and co-trimoxazole 960 mg daily without missed doses, but admits he occasionally forgets the fluconazole.

His prior meningitis workup at the outside hospital was reportedly negative for cryptococcal antigen and tuberculosis, though detailed records are not available. He has no history of seizures, but his wife describes two brief episodes over the past week where he appeared to stare blankly and his arms stiffened for approximately 30 seconds before returning to baseline, which she attributed to fatigue. He has not had any witnessed generalized tonic-clonic seizures. He has not traveled outside his usual routes in the past six months and has no known sick contacts with tuberculosis.

neurological_exam.additional: Nuchal rigidity present with resistance to passive neck flexion. Kernig sign positive bilaterally. Brudzinski sign positive. No rash, petechiae, or purpura on full skin examination. An ulcerated lesion approximately 1.5 cm in diameter noted on the right buccal mucosa near the molar region, present for approximately 3 weeks per patient report. A firm, mildly tender right submandibular lymph node approximately 2 cm in diameter is palpated. Mild right-sided jaw swelling noted, patient attributes to biting his cheek during a recent episode of teeth clenching at night.
neurological_exam.coordination: Finger-to-nose intact bilaterally without dysmetria. Heel-to-shin intact bilaterally. Rapid alternating movements normal.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils equal, round, reactive to light bilaterally (3 mm to 2 mm). No papilledema on fundoscopic exam. Visual fields full to confrontation. Extraocular movements intact, no nystagmus. Facial sensation intact bilaterally to light touch and pinprick. Facial movements symmetric at rest and with activation. Hearing grossly intact bilaterally. Palate elevates symmetrically. Sternocleidomastoid and trapezius strength 5/5 bilaterally. Tongue midline without fasciculations.
neurological_exam.gait: Gait steady with normal base and arm swing. Tandem gait intact. Romberg negative.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert but appears confused and mildly agitated. GCS 15 (E4 V5 M6). Oriented to person and place but initially gives incorrect date, self-corrects. Speech is fluent but tangential at times with occasional inappropriate laughter. Attention impaired: unable to spell WORLD backwards, manages only 3 serial 7s before losing track. Recall 2/3 objects at 5 minutes, recalls third with phonemic cue. Appears disinhibited, making inappropriate comments during examination.
neurological_exam.motor: Normal bulk throughout. Tone normal in upper and lower extremities. Strength 5/5 in all muscle groups tested bilaterally (deltoids, biceps, triceps, wrist extensors, finger abductors, iliopsoas, quadriceps, hamstrings, tibialis anterior, gastrocnemius). No pronator drift. No involuntary movements.
neurological_exam.reflexes: 2+ and symmetric at biceps, triceps, brachioradialis, patellar, and Achilles bilaterally. Plantar responses flexor bilaterally.
neurological_exam.sensory: Intact to light touch, pinprick, vibration, and proprioception in all extremities. No sensory level. No extinction to double simultaneous stimulation.
